title: Subset Sum below the meet-in-the-middle exponent
formal: Do there exist constants \(\varepsilon\in(0,1/2)\), \(c\ge1\) and a uniform classical bounded-error randomized algorithm deciding whether a subset of \(n\) positive integers sums to a nonnegative integer target in \(O(2^{(1/2-\varepsilon)n}L^{c})\) worst-case time, where \(L\) is the total binary input length?
why: A fixed worst-case exponent improvement would break one of the best-known barriers for exact algorithms on a fundamental weakly NP-complete problem.
status_note: Sources and subsequent-result searches checked on 13 September 2026. The cited results leave this target unanswered; this is a bounded literature review, not an exhaustive certification of current openness. Completes the existing draft TCS-4790 as the user-approved fixed exponent-saving target. Randomization, input encoding and exponential-space addressing are explicit; word operations on at most linear-in-input-bit-length words affect only polynomial factors.

definitions: The input is \(n\ge1\), a target \(t\ge0\), and an explicitly listed multiset \(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}\) of positive integers, all in binary with delimiters; \(L\) is the bit length of that full encoding. Accept if and only if there is \(I\subseteq[n]\) with \(\sum_{i\in I}x_{i}=t\). Each index is used at most once, repetitions of values are permitted, and the empty subset is allowed. Use a uniform random-access machine with \(w=d(n+\lceil\log_{2}(L+2)\rceil)\)-bit words for fixed \(d\ge1\), large enough to address exponential memory. Unit-cost instructions are word read/write, copy, arithmetic modulo \(2^{w}\), integer quotient and remainder with nonzero divisor, comparisons, Boolean operations and shifts; shifts by at least \(w\) return zero. Multiword integers are handled through charged component operations. Input packing, preprocessing and memory initialization are charged. Random words are independent and uniform and cost one instruction each. A fixed finite program receives no advice or tables. It answers correctly with probability at least \(2/3\) on every input and the time bound holds on every random execution. Constants are independent of all input values and \(n,L\). Quantum operations and random-instance promises are absent.

context_blocks.text: Meet-in-the-middle gives the classical half-exponent benchmark for worst-case Subset Sum. The target asks for a fixed positive saving in that exponent while allowing polynomial dependence on the input bit length.
The original saved question appears in a quantum-algorithms paper but explicitly concerns classical worst-case computation. Quantum and random-instance improvements do not answer that question.

Chan’s SODA 2026 introduction retains the worst-case exponential gap while resolving a pseudopolynomial derandomization question. A threshold-dependent algorithm can still be slow when numbers have large binary encodings.
A polynomial-factor speedup over the half-exponent bound is also insufficient: the requested saving is a fixed constant in the exponent, uniformly over all instances.

answer_criterion: Prove the stated existence claim or its logical negation, with the specified model, quantifiers and guarantees. A conditional lower bound settles only its conditional claim. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean; a partial improvement does not meet the target.

sentences: Subset Sum asks whether some subcollection of given positive integers adds to a target.
The classical worst-case benchmark comes from the meet-in-the-middle exponent.
The question asks for a fixed positive saving in that exponent with polynomial dependence on binary input length.
Bounded-error classical randomization is allowed, with no random-instance promise.
Quantum, pseudopolynomial and polynomial-factor improvements do not establish this fixed exponent saving.
